title: A method that predicts realistic chemical outcomes before the experiment

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable, affordable way to predict what a proposed chemical experiment will do before carrying it out: which products will form, in what proportions, how quickly, and through which competing pathways. Its intended reach includes diverse molecules and materials under realistic conditions, where solvents, interfaces, transition metals, and breaking or forming bonds can determine the outcome. This is the target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied studies.

The concept is defined by predictive performance rather than a particular computational method. Quantum calculations, empirical learning, or a combination could contribute. Fast, accurate calculations of electronic energies would be valuable, but realistic outcomes also depend on environmental effects, the configurations a system explores, competing pathways, and kinetics. Even an exact electronic Schrödinger-equation solution for hundreds of atoms would therefore be a component of the capability rather than a sufficient demonstration of it. Desktop execution is not essential; the relevant requirement is useful accuracy at a practical computational cost.

significance.text: Reliable prediction would let researchers make much stronger decisions about which reactions, catalysts, and conditions deserve experimental effort. The supplied inorganic-materials study identifies expensive trial and error as a discovery bottleneck. Extending dependable prediction across realistic chemical reactions could reduce that burden by screening alternatives before synthesis and identifying promising experiments with clearer expectations about products and competing outcomes.

As an interpretive analogy, such a capability could give chemistry a general working language in the broad sense that calculus gave science a language for continuous change: a way to turn proposed situations into quantitative predictions. The analogy concerns explanatory and predictive power. It does not imply that one compact formalism would make every chemical problem easy, or that a successful prediction engine must solve all underlying equations exactly.

Conditional downstream possibilities include faster development of medicines, catalysts, manufacturing processes, and functional materials. Those benefits would require additional work: experimental confirmation, synthesis routes, process engineering, safety assessment, and scale-up. A prediction could guide whether to pursue a reaction or material, but would not by itself establish that the resulting medicine works, that a plant is economical, or that a device is manufacturable.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved target is dependable prediction across a much broader range of chemistry than the bounded successes documented here. Many-electron calculations face a rapidly growing space of electronic configurations, while higher-accuracy wavefunction methods can become prohibitively expensive. Lee and Dieng describe this computational difficulty and motivate the search for faster predictions of unfamiliar molecules and materials.

A further barrier is physical generalization: a method must remain dependable when chemical composition, bonding, charge, geometry, or environment departs from its familiar examples. Lee and Dieng report striking failures in tested learned models. Merchant and colleagues, however, report useful transfer to selected unseen inorganic-material systems. Together these findings support a differentiated picture: generalization is possible within some tasks, but success there does not establish reliability across reactions, interfaces, and molecular chemistry.

Engineering synthesis: a complete outcome predictor would need to connect electronic structure with environmental sampling and reaction dynamics. It would have to find relevant pathways, compare their free-energy barriers under specified conditions, and translate competition among them into rates and product distributions. Reliable uncertainty estimates and recognition of unfamiliar cases would also matter in practice. An accurate energy for one chosen structure, or a correct ranking of a few supplied candidates, addresses only part of this task.

The supplied evidence does not establish a comprehensive field-wide absence of the target capability as of November 1, 2026. It documents important obstacles and bounded achievements at particular dates. The broader availability question remains open within this record because no assessment of later developments was supplied.

current_state.text: In their 2025 preprint, Siwoo Lee and Adji Bousso Dieng describe G4(MP2) as predicting molecular energies within about 1 kcal/mol of experiment for first-, second-, and third-row main-group elements. They also describe the steep computational scaling of higher wavefunction methods such as CCSD(T). This is evidence of useful accuracy for a defined class of molecular energies; it does not establish comparable accuracy for transition-metal catalysis, condensed-phase barriers, or quantitative product distributions.

The same preprint reports that the tested foundation models fail to reproduce the repulsive energy curve of two bare protons. Four tested models had been trained using more than 101 million structures; AIMNet2 instead used 20 million calculations. The authors interpret the failures as evidence that scaling training data alone is insufficient for reliable quantum chemical modeling. This remains an attributed result from a preprint about specified models and tests, not evidence that every learned model fails outside its training domain. The supplied assessment relied on the article's prose rather than independent inspection of its plotted curves.

On November 29, 2023, Merchant and colleagues reported GNoME results in Nature: 2.2 million crystal structures were computationally stable relative to the previous Materials Project reference, and 381,000 new entries remained on the updated convex hull. These are computational stability results under the study's reference framework. They do not establish that all those structures can be synthesized or remain stable under practical experimental conditions.

The GNoME study identified 736 matches between predicted structures and independently experimentally realized structures. Of those matches, 184 corresponded to experimental discoveries since the project's start. The 736 count is therefore neither a prospective synthesis success rate nor a report that GNoME predictions caused 736 syntheses.

GNoME also showed useful generalization on selected tasks involving unseen compositions, melted structures, and structures containing vacancies. Its training domain nevertheless consisted of bulk inorganic crystals; the supplement explicitly limits expectations for surfaces, clusters, and organic systems. These achievements concern selected materials predictions and do not demonstrate general reaction prediction. The supplied assessment had full article text and methods, but did not independently inspect the figures. The supplementary representation was partial because extraction skipped some form content; its readable limitations paragraph supported this specific scope distinction.

The research also referred to enzyme design for selected model reactions after screening and attributed a caution about computational proposals versus discoveries to Antypov, Rosseinsky, and colleagues. The supplied evidence does not verify either assertion, so neither establishes an additional demonstrated result here. The underlying distinction remains useful as a synthesis: proposing a structure computationally and experimentally establishing its realization are different achievements. Lack of verification in this record does not show that the cited assertions are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: evaluate a fixed method, without refitting, on a pre-registered set of unseen condensed-phase reactions that includes transition-metal catalysis and competing pathways. Before revealing experimental outcomes, specify the alternatives being compared and require predictions of the major product, the direction of selectivity between those alternatives, and barrier rankings. Pre-specify acceptable performance, uncertainty treatment, and computational budgets. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Unrefitted method predicts preregistered unseen reaction outcomes and barrier rankings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed stronger demonstration: extend the evaluation to quantitative reaction rates and product distributions across varied solvents, conditions, and chemical families. Test cases that require discovering relevant competing pathways as well as cases where alternatives are supplied. Where materials and interfaces are claimed within scope, include dedicated evaluations for them. Success on a finite reaction set would demonstrate breadth over that tested scope; it would not prove reliability for arbitrary molecules, materials, or environments.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Quantitative rates and product distributions across varied chemical conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent groups should be able to repeat the predictions and experimental comparisons using a documented model version, inputs, conditions, and computing resources. Evaluation should distinguish uncertainty in the measurements from prediction error, report failures and excluded cases, and examine whether reported confidence tracks actual reliability. Useful computational cost should be defined for the intended application rather than equated with desktop runtime.
completion_criteria.label: Independent groups reproduce predictions and comparisons with documented practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: The approximately 1 kcal/mol energy accuracy discussed for G4(MP2) provides context for one main-group molecular method. It does not supply a universal pass mark for catalytic barriers, selectivity, or rates. Proposed tolerances should instead be justified against the particular experimental decisions and quantities being predicted; correct qualitative rankings alone would not establish accurate quantitative kinetics.
completion_criteria.label: Prediction tolerances justified against experimental decisions and predicted quantities

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request for arbitrary reactions, and CHEMREV-09, phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids, are especially close applications. Chemical prediction could help evaluate catalytic pathways or anticipate material stability and competing phases. Their completion would additionally require producing effective catalysts or reliably making phase-pure solids. CHEMREV-01 concerns prediction; those entries concern realizing particular chemical capabilities. Only their titles were supplied, so more specific dependencies cannot be established.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-04, practical on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules, and CHEMREV-11, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond in a complex molecule, overlap through reaction planning and selectivity. General outcome prediction could guide route selection and the choice of conditions for a targeted bond. Practical synthesis also requires executing the route, while CHEMREV-11 demands a particular site-selective transformation. CHEMREV-10, positional manufacture of macroscopic atomically specified matter, could likewise benefit from predictions of local reactions, but requires control of assembly and manufacture beyond predicting outcomes.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-06, mild nitrogen fixation competitive with Haber–Bosch; CHEMREV-07, fossil-competitive multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water; CHEMREV-12, mild selective methane-to-methanol conversion; and CHEMREV-13, economical plastics-to-monomer recycling, are specific reaction and process goals. Better prediction could help identify catalysts, competing pathways, and operating conditions for each. Their defining conversion, selectivity, energy, and economic requirements would still need to be demonstrated in working processes.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-03, a manufacturable ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor, and CHEMREV-08, an aviation-relevant rechargeable air-breathing battery, could benefit from predictions of material stability, interfacial reactions, degradation, and synthesis outcomes. Their defining superconducting or battery performance would require additional physical modeling and experimental demonstration. General chemical prediction would not by itself establish either device-level capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CHEMREV-02, open-ended Darwinian evolution in a synthetic chemical system, could use reaction prediction to investigate candidate chemistries and environments. Its central achievement would be sustained evolutionary behavior in a physical chemical system. Predicting individual reactions would provide supporting knowledge without establishing open-ended evolution.

unresolved_issues: No freshness assessment was supplied for developments after the cited 2023 and 2025 studies; field-wide availability through November 1, 2026 remains unassessed.
The attributed Antypov–Rosseinsky statement and enzyme-design assertion remain unverified within the supplied evidence.
Benchmark composition, numerical success thresholds, uncertainty rules, and application-specific computational budgets remain to be defined.
Detailed descriptions of the other roster entries were not supplied. Their relationships are inferred from titles, rather than established from reviewed technical records.

The source index lists no extraction issues for the GNoME supplement, while the supplied evidence review reports skipped form content. The final record conservatively preserves the review's partial-extraction limitation.

brief.title: Reliable forecasts of chemical experiments
possible: Researchers could know what a proposed chemical experiment would produce before running it: which substances would form, in what proportions, and how quickly. They could compare competing routes to those products under realistic conditions, at a practical computing cost.
why: Researchers could spend less effort on expensive trial and error and choose more promising experiments. Better choices about reactions, catalysts—substances that speed reactions—and conditions could help develop medicines, manufacturing processes and useful materials.

sources.who: Siwoo Lee and Adji Bousso Dieng
sources.showed: In a preprint, they found that tested learning models failed basic tests of how energy changes as atoms separate. Increasing training data and model size did not reliably resolve those failures.
sources.quote: The models improve modestly only when non-ground-state structures are included in the training set.
sources.cited_for: Their tests show why success on familiar examples does not establish reliable predictions for unfamiliar chemistry.
sources.not_established: Failures in these tested models do not establish that every learned model will fail on unfamiliar chemistry.

sources.showed: Their GNoME learning system identified 381,000 new crystal structures that calculations placed among the stable candidates after comparison with competing structures.
sources.quote: Of the stable structures, 736 have already been independently experimentally realized.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates useful prediction of crystal stability and some success beyond familiar training examples.
sources.not_established: Calculated stability does not establish that a crystal can be made, and crystal predictions do not establish general reaction prediction.

shown: Merchant and colleagues used GNoME to predict stable inorganic crystals. Their predictions matched 736 structures independently made in experiments. Those matches do not measure how often a new prediction leads to a successful synthesis.

Accurate molecular energy calculations already work for defined classes of molecules. But Lee and Dieng’s preprint found basic failures in tested learning models. Neither result demonstrates dependable forecasts of complete chemical experiments.
missing: A dependable method must connect molecular energies, surrounding conditions and competing reaction routes to predict complete experimental outcomes.
Predictions must remain reliable when composition, bonding or surroundings differ from familiar examples, with confidence estimates that flag unfamiliar cases.
Broad experimental comparisons must establish useful accuracy and computing costs across reactions, materials and the boundaries where substances meet.

milestones.label: A fixed method predicts unseen reaction outcomes
milestones.explanation: An unchanged method would have to pass a preregistered test of unseen reactions in liquids, including transition-metal catalysts, predicting major products, preferences and energy-hurdle rankings. This would test prediction without refitting.

milestones.label: Accurate rates and product mixtures across varied conditions
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to predict rates and product proportions across solvents and reaction families, discovering competing routes and testing materials and surfaces where claimed. This would establish breadth within the tested scope.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat predictions and experiments with documented inputs and computing costs, separating measurement error from prediction error and testing confidence. This would establish reliability and practical limits.

milestones.label: Accuracy requirements match experimental decisions
milestones.explanation: Acceptable errors would have to be justified for each predicted quantity and experimental decision. This would prevent correct rankings from being mistaken for accurate reaction rates.

uncertain: Which reactions, success thresholds and confidence rules would make a convincing test remains open.
Useful computing costs and acceptable prediction errors depend on the intended experimental decision.

page.title: Quantitative chemical reaction outcome prediction
page.definition: A computational method predicts products, amounts over time, reaction rates and competing pathways from starting materials and specified experimental conditions. It works across reaction families in solutions, materials and interfaces, the boundaries between phases.

goal.need: Reaction forecasts must identify competing pathways as well as their rates. The DOE chemistry panel's material-aging example connects barrier-energy errors to orders-of-magnitude uncertainty in rates and requires atomistic representations of disorder and interfaces. These requirements explain why predicting one molecular energy or a stable structure does not establish the outcome of an experiment.

completion.title: Independent experiments validate complete reaction predictions across chemical families and environments.
completion.criterion: A fixed method predicts previously unmeasured reactions across different reaction families in solutions, materials and interfaces, including families outside its fitted domain. Independent laboratories confirm product identities, amounts over time and rates within stated experimental uncertainties, and experimentally distinguish its competing-pathway predictions. Predictions precede measurement and specify temperature, pressure, starting concentrations and environment. This is a provisional Atlas test; the searched sources supply no common sample size, breadth requirement or computing-cost limit.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional operationalization of the National Research Council's unknown-reaction prediction goal.
completion.basis: Searched NRC chemistry roadmaps, DOE Computational Chemical Sciences calls and grand-challenge reports, DARPA Make-It material, and reaction-prediction benchmark and blind-challenge literature for an integrated experimental acceptance test. No cross-domain pass criterion was located. This provisional test requires prospective experimental confirmation of the NRC's pathways-and-rates objective; the intermediate energy targets do not establish complete outcomes.

milestones.title: Molecular thermochemistry reaches a mean absolute error below 1 kcal/mol against experiment.
milestones.criterion: A method has a mean absolute deviation below 1 kcal/mol on the G3/05 molecular-energy benchmark. G4 reported 0.83 kcal/mol across its 454 experimental energies on 28 February 2007. The benchmark includes formation enthalpies, ionization energies, electron affinities, proton affinities and hydrogen-bond energies. Meeting this average does not bound every individual error or establish reaction rates.
milestones.set_by: Gaussian-n thermochemistry developers, Curtiss, Redfern and Raghavachari, Gaussian-4 theory, Section III; their stated accuracy target is assessed through benchmark average absolute deviations.

milestones.title: Solution-phase activation barriers reach a mean absolute prediction error below 1 kcal/mol.
milestones.criterion: For a specified solution-phase reaction family, predicted activation free energies—the free-energy barriers governing rates—have a mean absolute error below 1 kcal/mol against experiment. Jorner and colleagues reported 0.77 kcal/mol for nucleophilic aromatic substitution in their paper published online on 5 November 2020. They modeled 443 kinetic records and reserved 20% for testing. This establishes retrospective performance within that reaction family.
milestones.set_by: Reaction-kinetics chemical-accuracy convention, explicitly adopted by Jorner and colleagues in Chemical Science; their demonstration concerns nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

milestones.title: Reactive molecular dynamics reaches micrometre and microsecond scales at 1 kcal/mol accuracy.
milestones.criterion: Reactive molecular dynamics, which follows atoms while permitting bond changes, operates at micrometre and microsecond scales with 1 kcal/mol chemical accuracy. The DOE panel specifies neither an error statistic nor a validation set. On 29 November 2023, GNoME reported 50 ps simulations at 1,000 K for 623 unseen crystal compositions, which do not establish this target. Lee and Dieng's 30 September 2025 preprint, not peer reviewed, reports that five tested learned potentials fail the repulsion test for two bare protons.
milestones.set_by: DOE NNSA–ASCR workshop chemistry panel, priority research direction 3, page 74; this target was written for reactive simulations of materials.
milestones.threshold_quote: micron/microsecond scale with a chemical accuracy of 1 kcal/mol.

milestones.title: A method prospectively predicts products, amounts and rates within one reaction family.
milestones.criterion: A method fixed before test outcomes are measured predicts product identities, amounts over time and reaction rates for a specified reaction family and environment. Experiments confirm those predictions within stated experimental uncertainties and distinguish its competing-pathway predictions. This is a single-domain demonstration before cross-domain independent validation. Bradshaw and colleagues' 2025 benchmark instead tests recovery of recorded major products; it does not establish this integrated endpoint.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas, provisionally; searches of NRC and DOE goals and reaction-prediction benchmark protocols located no published joint-outcome acceptance threshold for this stage.

not_found: No external acceptance criterion was located for joint predictions of products, amounts, rates and pathways across chemical families and environments.
No published joint-outcome pass criterion was located for the single-family prospective demonstration.
No common sample-size requirement or computing-cost limit was located for complete reaction-outcome prediction.
The 2026 review An overview of reaction outcome prediction with physics-based and data-driven methods could not be opened.

results.finding: Five learned potentials incorrectly predict a system of two bare protons to be stable by approximately 500 kcal/mol.
results.detail: The static energy test exposes a failure of proton repulsion; it does not demonstrate reactive molecular dynamics at the required scales or accuracy.
results.quote: All models incorrectly predict this system can be extremely stable.

results.finding: GNoME potentials were used in molecular-dynamics simulations of 623 unseen compositions.
results.detail: The simulations assessed ionic-conductor classification against ab initio molecular dynamics. The text does not establish reactive dynamics at micrometre and microsecond scales or 1 kcal/mol accuracy.
results.quote: We use GNoME potentials pretrained on datasets of increasing size in molecular-dynamics simulations on 623 never-before-seen compositions.

results.finding: G4 achieved a mean absolute deviation of 0.83 kcal/mol across 454 G3/05 experimental energies.
results.detail: Several correction parameters were optimized against the G3/05 test set. The paper reports that 35 of the 454 energies had errors greater than 2 kcal/mol.
results.quote:
The results in Table II indicate that for the 454 energies,
the average absolute deviation from experiment at the G4
level is 0.83 kcal/ mol, which is a signiﬁcant improvement
over 1.13 kcal/ mol for the G3 theory.

results.finding: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution: 443 kinetic records modeled; test-set activation-barrier MAE was 0.77 kcal/mol.
results.detail: The data were randomly split 80% for model selection and 20% for testing. The result establishes retrospective performance within this reaction family.
results.quote:
We train a Gaussian Process Regression model to reproduce high-quality experimental kinetic data for the nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction and use it to predict barriers with a mean absolute error of 0.77 kcal mol
−1
for an external test set.

results.finding: FLARE reactive MD of H/Pt with 1 million atoms ran for 320 ps.
results.detail: A separate 1-billion-atom system had a 2.2 × 1.9 µm Pt surface, but the text does not establish microsecond-scale reactive MD at 1 kcal/mol accuracy.
results.quote: The final simulation time is 320 ps
